newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians reject Israeli redeployment plan.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians reject Israeli redeployment plan.

text.p: The Palestinian self-rule Authority (PA), accusing Israel of dictating peace, said it would reject officially on Sunday Israeli plans to hand over nine percent of the West Bank in a pending redeployment.

"We want the Israelis to stop the policy of dictation," PA peace negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters before a scheduled meeting at a Jerusalem hotel between a Palestinian delegation and Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy.
"The Israelis requested this meeting and we will submit our rejection officially," Erekat said. "We must decide the scope and the dimension of the redeployment together."

His comments were the latest expression of growing Palestinian anger over Israel's plans to build more Jewish housing in Arab East Jerusalem and implementation of a three-stage pullback from mainly rural areas of the West Bank.
In Gaza, a senior PLO official close to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said the time for passive resistance to Israel's settlement policy was over.

"The danger surrounding us is forcing us to decide whether to be free and masters over our land or slaves of the Israelis," Ahmed Abdel Rahman, general-secretary of Arafat's cabinet, said in a fiery speech in self-ruled Gaza.

"From now on, resisting settlements will not be through words, condemnation or complaints to the U.N. Security Council," he told a rally organised by the Islamic National Committee to Resist Settlements and the Palestinian Information Ministry.

Arafat condemned on Saturday a U.S. veto of a U.N. Security Council resolution calling on the Jewish state to abandon a plan to build homes for Jews at East Jerusalem's Jabal Abu Ghneim hill, which Israel calls Har Homa.
Erekat slammed Israel's decision on Friday to hand over nine percent of the West Bank as a violation of a September 1995 peace agreement. Arafat has called the move an Israeli trick.
But he conceded Israel could implement the redeployment unilaterally: "If they say they that I will not be surprised."

Going into the meeting with the Palestinians, Levy, asked what Israel's response would be to rejection of its redeployment plan, said: "Everything you say is 'if, if, if'. Why are we meeting? In order to overcome the 'if'."
The Authority insists under the 1995 deal the first redeployment, expected this week, was to cover 30 percent of the area still controlled by Israel in the West Bank.
Israel has said a U.S. note attached to a deal signed in January put the extent of the pullback at its sole discretion.
Despite its strong criticism, the PA has refrained from setting any conditions for continuing peace talks. Negotiations on a permanent peace deal are due to start later this month.

Levy's office said he had cancelled a planned trip to the United States because he and Netanyahu "decided the first priority is to continue the contacts with the Palestinians at the highest level". He had been slated to leave on Sunday night.
On the domestic front, Netanyahu remained under pressure from Israeli hawks who said the right-wing leader was being too generous in handing over territory to the Palestinians.

"I believe we should divorce Netanyahu and do everything so that this government is wound up as fast as possible," said Pinhas Wallerstein, head of the Council of Jewish Settlements in the West Bank and Gaza, after the group met on Sunday.
Eight legislators in Netanyahu's ruling coalition threatened to bolt the government over the redeployment.

But political analysts have said it was unlikely the rebels would carry out their threat for fear of forcing Netanyahu into forming a national unity government with the main opposition Labour party, which favours territorial compromise.
Israeli opposition leader Shimon Peres said his Labour party would not enter a unity government to protect Netanyahu from a right-wing rebellion over peace moves.
